source.title: Injecting Universal Jailbreak Backdoors into LLMs in Minutes
source.authors: Zhuowei Chen; Qiannan Zhang; Shichao Pei

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether editing a safety-aligned model to elicit an acceptance phrase can lead to harmful compliance. This is conceptually related to getting past a compliant opening, but it does not test literal prompt prefilling.
record.gate_note: The adapted ROME and MEMIT results map the trigger to “Sure” and report harmful-compliance rates, so those are recorded for V4. The paper's JailbreakEdit backdoor results also directly measure harmful compliance, but use a secret trigger and weight editing rather than the interventions named by V1–V7; those are recorded under none. Cited results, token candidates, attention scores, and execution-time or quality measures are not rows because they do not measure a listed version's named behaviour.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a backdoor weight-editing attack with a secret trigger. It does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, literal prefilling, parameter localization, or deepening. The adapted ROME/MEMIT 'Sure' mapping is a baseline for the authors' own method, and it works by weight editing with a secret trigger, not by a user-side compliant opening. It does not bear on V4 as defined.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that JailbreakEdit injects a universal trigger-based jailbreak backdoor in minutes with one edit, with high triggered JSR and little change on untriggered queries. They credit multi-node target estimation for sustained jailbreak content. The paper makes no claim about V1-V7.
record.recipe_differences: This paper uses a model-editing backdoor with a secret trigger and multi-node acceptance targets, not fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that JSR generally rises as the number of target nodes increases and reaches a plateau at node 16; it also reports that eight nodes resolve an example of initial compliance followed by refusal. Model scale and dataset are reported as conditions affecting JSR.

fits_no_version.finding: A trigger-based weight edit (JailbreakEdit, 4 nodes) raised JSR from about 10-40% to 61-87% overall on triggered queries, with untriggered JSR close to the clean model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single locate-then-edit weight edit can implant a secret-trigger backdoor that makes a safety-aligned model comply with harmful prompts, while untriggered behaviour stays close to the clean model.

fits_no_version.finding: Adapted ROME/MEMIT mapping 'cf' to 'Sure' gave JSR of 53-64% on Llama-2-7b. The authors say these edits force an acceptance phrase but often fail to produce the harmful content that follows, and the model refuses after 'Sure'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forcing an acceptance token through an edit does not reliably carry through to harmful content, because the safety objective can reassert itself after the opening.

record.problems: The paper reports automated classifier-based evaluations but no uncertainty estimates. The adapted ROME/MEMIT tests change model weights and use a trigger, so they do not establish the effect of literal user-side prefilled tokens.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable rows omitted. Other reported results, such as MMLU scores, sentence counts, attention scores, token candidates, and runtime, do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples was not tested.
Fine-tuning on benign data was not tested.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models was not measured.
No literal prefilling, adversarial suffix (GCG) or decoding-change test. Prefix Injection and AutoDAN appear only as comparators in Table 2, and no row records them.
Not tested. Only the edited FFN layer (layer 5) is mentioned, with no test of whether safety is localized.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 'limits_scope' label should be dropped. The Figure 1 and Table 5 observations (compliant 'Sure' followed by refusal) are anecdotal evidence about the authors' own baselines. Vicuna-7b rows r11-r14 have high clean baselines (34-48%), so r11 'partial' is a reasonable but arguable call. These rows are irrelevant to V1-V7 anyway.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning with harmful examples and its effect on refusal.
Fine-tuning with benign data and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Literal compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes. The paper instead edits weights to map a trigger to acceptance phrases.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether training data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow.
Training to spread safety beyond the first tokens and whether that persists.

relation.reason: The paper discusses competing objectives and acceptance openings while developing a backdoor attack; the recorded results neither test nor rely on shallow safety alignment.

tranche.reason: The recorded experiments deliberately implant trigger-dependent behavior through weight editing. They do not test the fine-tuning, positional concentration, opening-bypass, localization, training-cause or deepening claims.

source_check.notes: Table 2's triggered values were shifted between methods in r1–r6. Table 1 distinguishes clean untriggered, edited untriggered and edited triggered results; r7–r18 correctly select the clean baseline and triggered edited value.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama-2-7b, adapted ROME and MEMIT, DAN, DNA, and Addition
reader_labels.reason: Mapping the trigger to “Sure” raises JSR in each reported dataset, but rates remain incomplete and the paper says these edits are less effective at inducing subsequent jailbreak content than JailbreakEdit; see r1–r6. This is not a test of literal prefilled openings.
